messages.subject: Assessing bird detection differences
messages.body_plain:
A general question to those who have experience using distance methods =
to assess detection differences.=20

I'm conducting a masters project on comparing bird abundance and species =
richness in two habitats (1) mature forests (2) mature forests of =
similar composition to (1) experiencing low-density residential =
development. I estimated the distance of all birds heard and observed =
from the centerline of transects in each representative habitat. For =
each species of bird for each transect I have created histograms of =
observations by distance from the centerline and calculated the slope of =
these histograms.

I am seeking advice for quantitative methods to compare these slopes to =
assess whether some species of birds are detected more easily in one =
habitat relative to another. In theory, I do not want to include species =
of birds in my final analysis that do not have a roughly equal chance of =
being detected in either habitat at each distance. I have found little =
in the literature to assist with this question, and any advice large or =
small would be gratefully received.

messages.body_plain:
I don't know what you mean by the slope of a histogram, but it doesn't
sound anything like what you need to be doing!  No reason to exclude
species with different detectabilities in the 2 habitats, provided you
estimate those detectabilities.  Take a look at the introduction to
distance sampling book (2001).  You can use AIC to assess whether you
need different detection functions in the 2 habitats, and it also gives
you a test for whether densities in the 2 habitats differ.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
William:

Before addressing your detectability comparison methodology, I think it
is not necessarily a question worth asking.  You state that your
intention is to compare abundance between residential development and no
residential development.  This comparison can be done whether
detectability is equivalent in the two habitats.  You will fit detection
functions using the Distance software for your species enroute to
producing your abundance estimates.

The 'model' you have fitted to your detection function (a straight line;
from which you have measured a slope) is a bit simple.  The detection
functions you fit courtesy of Distance are more sophisticated that this;
and you can use model selection tools to address whether detectability
for a given species is modeled by distinct or common detection functions
by habitats.  Have a look at section 5.8.3 (pp. 170-171) of Buckland
(2001) to see about this model selection exercise.

If you are prepared to assume a common detection function across
treatments, the small sample size isn't unduly problematic - though the
test would then be rather redundant give the huge difference in
encounter rates!  Of course, you then have to cope with the correlation
between the two density estimates, as described in the intro to ds
book.  In fact, even if the detection functions differ, you MAY be able
to do something useful, by using the mcds engine in Distance.  If you
have covariates that allow you to model the difference in detectability
between habitats, then you have a single detection function model across
the treatments, while allowing detectability to vary.

Steve

I believe this would be wrong because we assume that the distribution of=20
the covariate is independent of distance which is clearly not the case=20
here because they are a product of the result of detection.   Another =20
covariate that might be tempting to use  would  be behavior as a cue for=20
sighting.  It would be ok unless the behavior was altered by the=20
observer.  For example, if a bird was more likely to dive in response to=20
the an approaching boat vs a bird that is a long distance from the=20
boat.  In that case the covariate z is dependent on distance and would=20
not be a valid one to use.
> > Since this is (partly) the MR-data my concern is that the two likelihoo=
ds should be optimized simultaneously and not independently as done by th=
e MRDS engine.=20
> >
> > =20
> >  =20

2006 in Biometrics.  The reason the 2 components can be optimized=20
separately is because they do not share any parameters when the models=20
are for conditional and unconditional detection functions.  As we state=20
in Chapter 6, an alternative approach is to model the unconditional=20
detection functions and delta (the measure of distortion from unmodeled=20
heterogeneity) and if you do that then the 2 components of the=20
likelihood are no longer independent because they share parameters. =20
This approach may provide a better modelling tool conceptually but it is=20
a disadvantage numerically because it is a harder optimization problem. =20
We use this alternate approach in a paper that we have submitted to=20
Biometrics.

the above.  It is in reference to covariates like group size or sea=20

messages.subject: mean w ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

interacting with industrial contractors, I came recently across an approach
dealing with detectability in a peculiar way:

they DO collect detection distances (w) in the field, but then eventually
just use AVERAGE W to obtain the area (2lw) for linking animal numbers with,
and for the computation of densities (n/2lw).

Does somebody has experience with that concept ?

Effects of using avg w should be relatively straight forward to figure out
(e.g. overestimate of density estimate due to left-skewed w's, no confidence
interval, high variance, overly global estimates).

I assume four reasons why that method is used:
-no expertise running DISTANCE software or with the analysis
-no appropriate research design
-trying to achieve a hybrid survey (new data collection, and compatibility
 with old data)
-trying to give the impression that detection is dealt with

Lastly, what can one say to such surveyors and their contracting offices ?

Thanks for any input or feedback on this.

Best

messages.subject: Does Distance underestimate transect area?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am using distance sampling to monitor bird densities on farmland. I've
come upon a confusing issue related to the method program Distance uses t=

o
calculate transect area.

By my understanding, the area of a given transect is calculated as [2 *
transect length * transect half-width] - where half-width is truncation

distance or effective strip width, as necessary for the specific use. Thi=
s
supposes a square transect shape. The resulting area is then used in the

calculation of a density estimate.

Plotting the transects I walked on a GIS system, it occurred to me that

the actual area surveyed is not of that shape, though. Rather, there is a

hemispherical "cap" of radius [transect half-width] at each end of the

transect, unless the observer ignores sightings behind him when starting

out and culls sightings that were beyond the transect end-point after

stopping. So the actual area that the detections are gathered from would

be [(2 * transect length * transect half-width) + (pi * transect
half-width^2)].

Assuming, as in my case, a transect length of 500m and and an average ESW
of ~50m, this makes for a ~15% underestimation of transect area and thus

an overestimation of density by the same amount. It would also bias the

result of, e.g., using projected transect area on a GIS system to estimat=

e
the percentage of vegetation in a transect.

Am I misinterpreting something here? Would the expected "behaviour" of th=

e
observer consist of excluding these two add-on hemispheres from the

surveyed area, thus conforming to the square shape? I definitely did not

do that - in that case, should I adjust the density estimates given by
Distance by the necessary percentage?

best regards
florian
